channel.title: Weekly Padgett
channel.description: Stories from thirty years of telecom billing mediation, Unix, corkscrew, bass guitar, Indonesian music, and whatever else Pat Padgett could not shut up about.

item.title: Never post twice. Yes, even when I run the damned thing twice.
item.description: grime95.com posts daily fiction to a website, Facebook and Instagram. Posting was easy. Keeping a retry from posting the same damned thing again took some work.
item.content:encoded:
You want a script that posts something once a day, forty lines should do it. Then you get to spend the next week figuring out what happens when those forty lines half-work.

I run grime95.com[1], a serialized fiction site publishing one fictional small-town booking record every day at noon Eastern. Each goes to a static site (a GitHub Pages[2] repo), a Facebook Page, and Instagram. Cron[3] does it. Twenty percent of that script took eighty percent of the thought, most of it about what could go wrong.

My billing mediation habit kicks in here, because I've spent a lot of time reconciling things and I want a ledger I can check. I used SQLite[4], one row per (entry, channel). Status: pending | success | uncertain.

Three statuses, because sometimes I genuinely don't know what happened.

When a POST to Meta's Graph API[5] throws, you don't know whether the post exists. Maybe it completed and the response disappeared. Maybe the token expired and nothing happened. Instagram takes two calls, create a container and publish it, so it can half-happen. A leftover container expires on its own, but isn't easily distinguished from one that published.

POSTs get exactly ONE attempt. An exception marks the row uncertain, and the script stops touching that (entry, channel) pair. On the next run, GETs retry freely. Reading is idempotent, so I can keep looking without posting another copy.

Every channel adapter gets a checkpoint callback. The instant it has a remote ID, it calls that callback.

Verification can fail. The process can get killed. The ledger already knows a post with that ID exists, so the next run sees remote_id and doesn't repost. Instagram checkpoints even the container ID as container:<id> before publishing. Half-done counts as something I want written down!!

About 480 lines of Python. Standard library plus Pillow[6] for image checks. I wrote it in an afternoon and I'm proud of the thing. Getting the failure states right took the week after.

I don't want to babysit it every day at noon.

References

  1. grime95.com: https://grime95.com/
  2. GitHub Pages: https://pages.github.com/
  3. Cron: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  4. SQLite: https://www.sqlite.org/
  5. Meta's Graph API: https://developers.facebook.com/docs/graph-api/
  6. Pillow: https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/

item.title: Billing mediation: somebody has to find the damned money
item.description: Fourteen years between the switch and the bill, finding missing money in binary records. What telecom mediation does, and why two bytes can ruin your day.
item.content:encoded:
You hear "billing mediation[1]" and probably picture me spending fourteen years looking at invoices. I understand, but there is a looooong way to go before an invoice exists, and I worked in the middle where a phone company either makes its money or quietly loses it.

The switch doesn't give a damn about your rate plan. It records the A-number, B-number, start time, duration, cell site, trunk group, cause code, and a few dozen other fields in a proprietary binary structure.

Billing needs somebody to translate that thing before it can rate it, which is where mediation comes in.

Collection means pulling files from 130 switches over whatever they support: FTP[2], X.25[3] on the old ones, a vendor-specific push. It runs on a schedule, and you verify every file in the sequence and SCREAM when a number is missing. The call already happened! That gap is unbilled revenue until somebody gets its record.

Then you parse the binary. Release 17 added a field and shifted everything after it by two bytes, and nobody told you. Two BYTES! Plenty of room to fuck up your afternoon.

Reconciliation means counting what came in against what went out at every stage, then explaining every difference. You don't get to shrug at the leftovers.

Over fourteen years I recovered tens of millions of dollars finding that shit. Mangled headers, truncated tails, sequence gaps, records rejected into an error queue nobody watched. It was hex dumps[4] and "why did this file stop at byte 48,201?" I am proud of that work, even if I mostly remember staring at hex dumps.

And I still want to look in that fucking error queue.

References

  1. billing mediation: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications_mediation
  2. FTP: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc959
  3. X.25: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X.25
  4. hex dumps: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hex_dump

item.title: Twenty-five years of corkscrew. All 291 damned lines.
item.description: I wrote 291 lines of C to get SSH through a corporate proxy in 2000. Linux distributions kept shipping it. Modern analysis has some things to tell me.
item.content:encoded:
I wrote corkscrew[1] in an afternoon. A quarter century later I'm still discussing it, although I would have preferred to be discussing something other than its stack buffer overflow.

In 2000 I was behind a corporate HTTP proxy that let port 443 out and nothing else. I wanted SSH access to my own machine at home. The proxy spoke HTTP CONNECT[2], SSH spoke a raw TCP stream, and OpenSSH[3] had this option nobody seemed to use, ProxyCommand. I wrote the thing to sit between them.

291 lines of C, folks. Debian[4], Ubuntu, Red Hat, CentOS, FreeBSD and Cygwin have packaged it. Linux Magazine and 2600 reviewed it. It has a Wikipedia article. An afternoon's work has an encyclopedia entry now!!! I certainly didn't expect that.

I recently had the source put through GCC[5] static analysis, AddressSanitizer[6], UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and a loopback mock proxy sending deliberately hostile responses. I wanted to know what 26-year-old C looks like under modern tooling, and, well... it looks like 26-year-old C. Fuck.

The big finding is a stack buffer overflow reachable from the proxy. The response handler does a read() into a 4096-byte buffer, doesn't add a terminator, and hands it to sscanf() with unbounded %s. Send 4096 non-whitespace bytes and you get a write one byte past the buffer. No code execution was demonstrated. A hostile proxy can still corrupt the client's stack, and I do not particularly enjoy typing that about MY software.

The framing bug bothers me more, because I can't blame a typo. The code treats the first read() as the whole proxy response, and on a 200 it throws all of it away. If headers and the first bytes of the SSH greeting arrive in the same segment, the greeting goes with them. And with fragmented headers it tries to parse HTTP/1. and exits.

It worked for 25 years because proxies almost always send headers in their own packet. I wrote that assumption into the thing, and now I get to look at it again.

The rest I'd leave alone. But those damned buffers need terminators.

References

  1. corkscrew: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corkscrew_(program)
  2. HTTP CONNECT: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-connect
  3. OpenSSH: https://www.openssh.com/
  4. Debian: https://www.debian.org/
  5. GCC: https://gcc.gnu.org/
  6. AddressSanitizer: https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html
